cells.tense: The pattern is in view, and you are moving, and the two feed each other.
cells.act: sketch the whole of it badly, on one page, and keep the sketch
cells.ask: Sketch the whole thing badly on one page — the goal, the ground it stands on, where you are on it. Keep it ugly. Then take the next move with only the light that sketch gives you.
cells.core:
You can see the whole pattern from where you stand, and you're still moving toward something. That pairing is what makes this worth saying: nothing has stalled in the watching, and the driving hasn't made you miss what's close by. You're moving from genuine interest, not momentum that won't stop. The picture of where you're heading is clear enough to steer and open enough to change when it needs to.

What carries this is imagining forward — not forcing the whole road into view, keeping a rough version of it somewhere you can glance at, and letting each step give you enough to take the next. You probably know how this feels when it's working. Where it may bend is wanting the full map before the first move. Enough for the next step is plenty, and that much is already yours.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the whole thing and still move.
cells.place: the overlook where the whole pattern shows

cells.tense: By the time you arrive anywhere, you are already past it, driving on.
cells.act: adjust one dial a little, then stop
cells.ask: Find the one dial that runs everything — pace, hours, output — and turn it down a notch. Then stop adjusting. Feel what the notch does over the next few days before you touch anything else.
cells.core:
The pattern is clear in your head and the destination keeps shifting ahead, so you speed up. The push has outrun the the thing it was supposed to reach. You're driving past rest stops, past the ones you love, past arrival itself. That's the shape right now, and it can be hard to see from inside because it feels like good momentum.

What rebalances here is tuning — not stopping, adjusting. Add a little, take a little away, and sense the difference before the next correction. You don't need a big change. Small, live adjustments and the willingness to feel them land. When this is working, you can feel where you are, and it's good. When it's bent, you can't feel it at all. One honest adjustment, then wait. Balance holds by staying in touch.

cells.tense: You stood at a door that is behind you now, and you didn't walk through.
cells.act: clear the space the ending leaves
cells.ask: Take the thing whose time has passed — a project, a role, a plan — and clear the room it kept. Move it off the desk, out of the calendar. Start nothing in the space it leaves.
cells.core:
You can see the pattern, all of it — what led here, what you meant to do, where it stopped. And the feet stay planted. What you notice is steady and the going isn't happening. A door sits behind you and you're turned toward it, waiting for something that's already gone to return. That isn't laziness. It's a motor stalling because a chapter didn't get declared finished.

What's asked is the ending that lets the next thing come: let what's over be over, without pushing yourself forward — you don't have that right now, and pressing the tired place is the wrong move. Clear the room the old form kept, then leave that space be and see what arrives. You've finished hard things before. This one is an ending, not a new beginning.
cells.sheetLine: The thing is over. You're still at its door.

cells.tense: The car is moving and you would say you are not the one steering.
cells.act: stop holding up the false thing and watch it come down
cells.ask: Pick the structure you keep upright by habit — a plan, a story, a routine — and stop holding it for a while. Watch what happens when you don't. Don't rush to fix anything that falls.
cells.core:
Forward motion and forward-looking eyes are already yours. What isn't clear is that you're the hand on it. The moves are yours and the account you give skips the author. Or the other way: standing still and saying there's no momentum, while something keeps steering anyway. Given how well you read the pattern, the question is whether the person doing the reading gets credit from the momentum doing the moving.

What breaks through is a false structure losing its prop: something is being held up by a habit. The habit is small — a ritual, a reassurance, a repeated check — and it's doing the work of appearing not to move. Let one such prop go and watch what it was bearing. No new plan is needed. Stop carrying the old structure and see what sits underneath.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering something and saying it drives itself.
